title: Seven Days Beneath Govardhana
story:
The storm did not pass. The rain that Indra had sent kept falling, and the people of Vrindavan had taken shelter in a strange place — the hollow beneath a mountain that a boy held up with one hand.

Krishna had uprooted Govardhana and lifted it over the cowherds like a great umbrella, and the villagers and their cattle had crowded beneath it, out of the torrent. But the refuge was not a comfortable one, and the days did not pass easily. Hunger and thirst pressed on them. Their bodies ached. The soft ground, the warm houses, the easy comfort of their own cow-pens — all of it was gone, and in its place there was only the dim space under the hill and the sound of the storm beyond it.

Yet Krishna would not let fear in. He told them plainly: there is nothing to fear here; the hill will not fall on you while I hold it. And so the villagers, their minds steadied by his word, went in and stayed. They set aside their hunger, their thirst, their aches, and their longing for comfort, and they remained beneath the mountain, their cattle and their families with them.

Day followed day, and Krishna did not move from his place. Seven days he stood there, holding the hill, and for seven days the people of Vraja lived in that shelter and found that it held. There was little to do beneath the mountain but wait and trust, and that, in the end, was what they learned to do. The hill above them never slipped. The arm beneath it never tired.

Then, at last, something changed. Indra had sent the storm, and Indra had been watching. As the seventh day turned, the king of the gods looked down and saw what had come of his fury — that the cowherds he meant to destroy were sheltered and dry beneath a mountain lifted by a cowherd boy, and that the boy had not stirred through all of it. Astonishment overtook his anger. He called back his clouds, and the storm began to break.

The rain slackened and stopped. The cruel wind died away. The clouds thinned and drew apart, and the sun came out again over a washed and shining Vrindavan. At last the word went round the shelter that the danger was over, and the cowherds were told to come out and leave their fear behind — all of them, with their women, their wealth, and their children. The refuge beneath the hill, which had been a shelter against what looked like the world's end, opened at last onto morning.

The cowherds looked at one another in the clear light. They had not been destroyed. The mountain had held, and the boy beneath it had not failed them.
reflection: The seven days beneath the hill are a test of endurance as much as a rescue. The cowherds surrender comfort, hunger, and fear at Krishna's word, and in exchange they learn that the refuge he offers can be trusted to hold.
next_story_tease: The storm had passed, and now the hill could be set down at last.
hero_scene: Krishna standing motionless for seven days holding Govardhana aloft on one raised hand, while cowherds, cattle, and families huddle in the dim, dry hollow beneath the mountain as rain lashes the world outside.
visual_elements: Krishna holding Govardhana on one hand
a mood of endurance and quiet trust
